references.text: The accusers elaborate on the charge that Jesus stirs up the people: "He stirs up the people with his teaching throughout all Judea" ([ref:Luk 23:5|Luke 23:5]).
Pilate summarizes the charges and clears Jesus of them: "You brought this man to me as one who is leading the people astray" ([ref:Luk 23:14|Luke 23:14]).
Also in Matthew, Jesus is brought before Pilate and asked if he is the king of the Jews, which corresponds to the charge that he called himself Christ, a king ([ref:Matt 27:11|Matthew 27:11]).
Mark's parallel account where Pilate asks Jesus: "Are you the king of the Jews?" and the chief priests accuse him of many things ([ref:Mark 15:2-3|Mark 15:2-3]).
In John's account, Pilate questions Jesus after the charge, and Jesus answers about the nature of his kingdom—an elaboration on the charge of making himself king ([ref:Joh 18:29-33|John 18:29-33]).
The charge that Jesus makes himself king is set against loyalty to the emperor: "Everyone who makes himself a king sets himself against the emperor" ([ref:Joh 19:12|John 19:12]).

The attempt to trap Jesus with the question about paying taxes to the emperor underlies the charge that he forbade paying taxes ([ref:Luk 20:20-25|Luke 20:20-25]). Jesus actually said the opposite: "Give to Caesar what belongs to Caesar."
The same type of charge is brought against Paul and Silas in Thessalonica: they act "against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, namely Jesus" ([ref:Apg 17:6-7|Acts 17:6-7]).
Paul is later accused in a similar way of being a troublemaker among Jews throughout the world, a parallel to the charge against Jesus of misleading the people ([ref:Apg 24:5|Acts 24:5]).
The angel announced that Jesus is "Christ, Lord"—Messiah and king—the true identity behind the charge that he called himself "Christ, a king" ([ref:Luk 2:11|Luke 2:11]).
Daniel's prophecy about the anointed prince (Messiah) who is to come, the background for Jesus' identity as "Christ, a king" ([ref:Dan 9:25|Daniel 9:25]).
